# 1. Introduction

installation of R and RStudio,
using R as a calculator, data importation, data description using numerical
measures and graphs, and data structures (vectors, factors, lists, data frames,
matrices and arrays).

Important definitions in data science: **Statistics, Modelling, Computation, Calculus**.

An R Markdown document can contain text and R code chunks. When we click **Knit**,
the code is run and its output is shown in the document, for example:

```{r cars}
summary(cars)
```

Plots can also be embedded. The option `echo = FALSE` hides the code and shows only the plot:

```{r pressure, echo=FALSE}
plot(cars, main = "Speed and stopping distance of cars")
```

# 2. Data structures

## Vectors

A vector is the foundational R data structure.

**Numeric**

```{r numeric}
x <- c(0.5, 0.6)
age <- c(20, 35, 32, 29)
summary(age)
```

```{r numeric2}
age <- c(35, 24, 18, 24)
mean(age)
```

**Logical, character, integer and complex**

```{r other-vectors}
x <- c(TRUE, FALSE)
x <- c(T, F)

x <- c("a", "b", "c")
class_gender <- c("M", "F", "F", "M")

x <- 9:29
x

x <- c(1+0i, 2+4i)
x
```

## Matrix and operations within matrices

```{r matrix}
(x <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3))
(y <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 3, ncol = 2))

x %*% y        # matrix multiplication
```

## List

```{r list}
(x <- list(1, "a", TRUE, 1 + 4i))
```

## Factor

```{r factor}
x <- factor(c("yes", "yes", "no", "yes", "no"))
x
levels(x)
table(x)
```

## Missing values (NA)

```{r na}
x <- c(1, 2, NA, 10, 3)
is.na(x)                 # logical vector showing which elements are NA
```

A value written as the text `"NA"` is **not** a real missing value:

```{r na-text}
x <- c(1, 2, 4, "NA", 5)
bad <- is.na(x)
print(bad)
x[!bad]
```

What if there are several R objects and we want the subset with no missing
values in any of them? We use `complete.cases()`:

```{r complete-cases}
x <- c(1, 2, NA, 4, NA, 5)
y <- c("a", "b", NA, "d", NA, "f")
good <- complete.cases(x, y)
good
x[good]
y[good]
```

## Coercion

If a character is present in a vector, R converts everything to character
strings. If a vector contains only logical values and numbers, R converts TRUE to 1
and FALSE to 0:

```{r coercion}
c(1, "a", TRUE)
sum(c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE))
```

# 3. Creating data

## Using a data frame

A data frame is more general than a matrix because it can contain different
modes of data (numeric, character, and so on), similar to a SPSS or SAS dataset.

```{r dataframe}
studentID  <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
math_score <- c(12, 17, 10, 9, NA)
gender     <- c("M", "F", "M", "M", "F")
it_score   <- c(13, 18, 11, 10, 19)

scoredata <- data.frame(studentID, gender, math_score, it_score)
scoredata
```

## Creating data from the keyboard

Steps: (1) create an empty data frame with variable names, (2) open the text
editor with `edit()`. This is interactive, so it is not run when knitting.

```{r keyboard, eval=FALSE}
data_class2 <- data.frame(height = numeric(0), weight = numeric(0), bmi = numeric(0))
data_class2 <- edit(data_class2)
```

# 4. Data importation

R can import data from different sources: text files, spreadsheets, statistical
packages (SAS, SPSS, Stata), web data (XML, web scraping) and database
management systems (SQL, MySQL, Oracle, Access).

## From a text file

```{r import-txt}
data_class <- read.table("class_data.txt", header = TRUE)

variable.names(data_class)
head(data_class)
tail(data_class)
data_class[10:20, ]
```

```{r txt-explore}
summary(data_class$WEIGHT)
length(data_class$WEIGHT)
data_class$WEIGHT
```

## From a dataset built into R

```{r builtin}
# data()   # lists the datasets currently available
data("airquality")
variable.names(airquality)
str(airquality)
```

## Homework 1: data from a statistical package and from a DBMS

**Statistical package (SPSS)**: my dataset `students.sav`, read with the **haven** package.

```{r hw-spss}
library(haven)

students <- read_sav("students.sav")
dim(students)

students_small <- students[, c("CNTRY", "AGEA", "GNDR", "STFLIFE", "TRSTPLT")]
head(students_small)
summary(students_small)
```

**Database management system**: the data is saved in a SQLite database with the
**DBI** and **RSQLite** packages and imported back with an SQL query.
(For MySQL only the `dbConnect()` line changes.)

```{r hw-db}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)

con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "class.sqlite")
dbWriteTable(con, "class_data", data_class, overwrite = TRUE)

dbListTables(con)
db_data <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM class_data WHERE HEIGHT > 165")
db_data

dbDisconnect(con)
```

# 5. Exploratory data analysis

## Numerical variables: common summaries

```{r eda-summary}
summary(data_class)
str(data_class)
```

## Summary statistics

```{r eda-apply}
apply(data_class, 1, mean)   # mean of each row
apply(data_class, 2, sd)     # standard deviation of each column

c(mean(data_class$HEIGHT), sd(data_class$HEIGHT))
c(mean(data_class$WEIGHT), sd(data_class$WEIGHT))

c(Mean = mean(data_class$HEIGHT), SD = sd(data_class$HEIGHT))
c(Mean = mean(data_class$WEIGHT), SD = sd(data_class$WEIGHT))
```

# 6. Variation and covariation

## Relationship between a categorical and a continuous variable

```{r iris}
data("iris")
head(iris)

mean(iris$Petal.Length)
mean(iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "setosa"])
mean(iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "versicolor"])
mean(iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "virginica"])
```

A shortcut using `by()`:

```{r iris-by}
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, mean)
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, sd)
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, summary)
```

Box-and-whisker plot to visualise differences between categories:

```{r iris-boxplot}
boxplot(iris$Sepal.Length ~ iris$Species, data = iris,
        main = "Comparison of categorical vs quantitative")
```

## Relationship between two categorical variables

```{r ucb}
ucba <- data.frame(UCBAdmissions)
head(ucba)

(cross <- xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = ucba))
```

Is there gender bias in the UC Berkeley graduate admission process?

```{r ucb-prop}
prop.table(cross, 1)
```

## Simpson's paradox

A trend that appears in combined groups of data can disappear or reverse when
the data is broken down into groups. In Department F, women were admitted at a
slightly higher rate than men:

```{r simpson}
cross2 <- xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = ucba[ucba$Dept == "F", ])
prop.table(cross2, 1)
```

# 7. Graphs

## Bar charts

```{r barplot1}
dat <- read.table(text = "ProdA ProdB ProdC ProdD
1 110 50 60 70
2 120 50 80 65", header = TRUE)

barplot(as.matrix(dat), beside = TRUE, col = c("Red", "green"),
        main = "Products by group")
```

```{r barplot2}
dat <- read.table(text = "A B C D E F G
1 10 80 30 90 70 60  90
2 20 50 70 50 40 10  40
3 60 80 80 60 60 30 160
4 20 40 70 80 20 10  70", header = TRUE)

barplot(as.matrix(dat), main = "Stacked bar chart")
```

## Scatter plots

```{r scatter}
plot(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)
plot(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT)
plot(data_class[, 1], data_class[, 2], main = "Graph")
```

```{r cor}
cor(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT)
```

# 8. Linear models

```{r lm-plot}
plot(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)
abline(lm(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)$coefficient)
```

```{r lm}
data_lm <- lm(HEIGHT ~ WEIGHT, data = data_class)
summary(data_lm)
```

Diagnostic plots of the model:

```{r lm-diagnostic, fig.show='hold', out.width='50%'}
plot(data_lm)
```

Histograms:

```{r hist}
hist(data_class$HEIGHT)
hist(data_class$WEIGHT, col = "blue")
```

Linear line together with a smooth (lowess) line:

```{r lm-lowess}
plot(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)
abline(lm(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)$coefficient)
lines(lowess(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT), col = "blue")

cor(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT)
lm(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)
```

**Interpretation:** the correlation is about 0.27 (weak and positive), and the
slope of 0.36 means that each extra centimetre of height is associated with
about 0.36 kg more weight. The relationship is weak (R-squared about 0.07, p-value about 0.08).

# 9. Data management

## Creating another variable (BMI)

```{r bmi}
BMI <- data_class$WEIGHT / (data_class$HEIGHT / 100)^2
BMI <- round(BMI, digits = 2)

head(cbind(data_class, BMI), n = 5)
new_data_class <- cbind(data_class, BMI)
tail(new_data_class, n = 10)
```

Summary of BMI:

```{r bmi-summary}
summary(BMI)
stem(BMI, scale = 2)
```

## Dates

```{r dates}
today <- Sys.Date()
format(today, format = "%B %d %Y")
format(today, format = "%A")

dob <- as.Date("1982-02-10")
difftime(today, dob, units = "days")

startdate <- as.Date("2004-02-13")
enddate   <- as.Date("2011-01-22")
enddate - startdate
```

# 10. Subsetting

We use `$`, `[ ]` and `[[ ]]`.

**Leadership data.** The study asks how men and women differ in the way they lead
their organisations. Five questions were asked (1 = strongly disagree,
2 = disagree, 3 = neither agree nor disagree, 4 = agree, 5 = strongly agree).
In the `age` variable, 99 means the value is missing.

```{r leadership}
manager <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
country <- c("US", "US", "UK", "UK", "UK")
gender  <- c("M", "F", "F", "M", "F")
age     <- c(32, 45, 25, 39, 99)
q1 <- c(5, 3, 3, 3, 2)
q2 <- c(4, 5, 5, 3, 2)
q3 <- c(5, 2, 5, 4, 1)
q4 <- c(5, 5, 5, NA, 2)
q5 <- c(5, 5, 2, NA, 1)

leadership <- data.frame(manager, country, gender, age, q1, q2, q3, q4, q5)
str(leadership)
names(leadership)
```

## Missing values and age categories

```{r recode}
leadership$age[leadership$age == 99] <- NA

leadership$agecat[leadership$age > 75] <- "Elder"
leadership$agecat[leadership$age >= 35 & leadership$age <= 75] <- "Middle Aged"
leadership$agecat[leadership$age < 35] <- "Young"

leadership
```

## Handling missing values

Listwise deletion removes all observations with missing data. (Another option is to
replace a missing value by the average of the remaining data.)

```{r na-omit}
is.na(leadership[, 5:9])

newdata <- na.omit(leadership)
newdata
```

## Sorting data

```{r sort}
order(leadership$age)
newdata2 <- leadership[order(leadership$age), ]
newdata2
```

## Merging data sets

`merge()` joins two data frames horizontally using a common key. `rbind()` joins
them vertically (they must have the same variables). Example:

```{r merge}
dataframeA <- data.frame(ID = c(1, 2, 3), country = c("US", "US", "UK"),
                         score = c(10, 20, 30))
dataframeB <- data.frame(ID = c(1, 2, 3), country = c("US", "US", "UK"),
                         age = c(32, 45, 25))

merge(dataframeA, dataframeB, by = "ID")                  # example 1
merge(dataframeA, dataframeB, by = c("ID", "country"))    # example 2

rbind(dataframeA, data.frame(ID = 4, country = "UK", score = 40))
```

## Selecting and dropping variables and observations

```{r subset}
newdata3 <- leadership[, c(5:9)]
myvars <- c("q1", "q2", "q3", "q4", "q5")
(newdata3 <- leadership[myvars])

(newdata4 <- leadership[, -(1:5)])
newdata5 <- leadership[, c(-1, -7)]

leadership[[4]]
leadership$age

newdata6 <- leadership[c(2, 4, 5), ]
newdata6

newdata7 <- subset(leadership, age >= 35 | age < 24, select = c(q1, q2, q3, q4, q5))
newdata7

(newdata8 <- leadership[leadership$gender == "M" & leadership$age > 30, ])
```
